feedback: If the child writes 21, 25, 29… or says 'just keep adding 4', note that this term-to-term habit works but won't reach the 100th term efficiently — tabulate position against term so the relationship (4×position + 1) is visible, then ask for the 100th term.

If the child scales a known term by the position ratio (e.g. says the 20th term = 4×the 5th term), test that shortcut against a known term: does 4×(the 1st term) give the 4th term correctly? (4×5 = 20, but the 4th term is 17.) Use the position table to show that scaling multiplies the constant start-offset too, so the result is too big.
If the child announces a rule but won't check it, ask 'does your rule give the 3rd term correctly? check it' so verification becomes a habit rather than an afterthought.
activities.intendedInsight: A position-to-term rule lets you reach any term in one step, which counting-on cannot do efficiently; a rule is only trustworthy once checked against a known term.
learnerActions: Look at a sequence such as 5, 9, 13, 17, … and notice the constant difference of 4.
Try to reach the 20th term by extending term-by-term and feel how slow and error-prone this gets.
Make a table pairing position (n) with term so the relationship becomes visible.
State a position-to-term rule (e.g. term = 4×position + 1) and use it to jump straight to the 20th term (81).
Check the rule against a known early term (does it give the 3rd term correctly?) before trusting it.
Then be asked for the 100th term, where listing is clearly impractical, so the general rule proves its worth.
activities.title: Sequence machine: force the jump to a far term

feedback: If the child treats each percentage as a separate calculation, prompt them to start from 10% (÷10) and 5% (half of 10%) and ask which combination of those parts makes the target.
If the child assembles 35% correctly, ask whether the same approach gives 65% so they generalise the method rather than memorising one case.
An optional 'builder' where 10% and 5% tiles snap together to make 35% can make the part-whole structure tangible, but a drawn percentage bar or a ratio table serves the same purpose.
activities.intendedInsight: Any multiple of 5% can be built by combining derived facts (10% and 5%) rather than treated as a separate one-off conversion. Other percentages, such as 37%, need further derived facts like 1%. This gives a reusable method that scales to any amount.
learnerActions: Find 10% of an amount by dividing by 10.
Find 5% by halving the 10% value.
Assemble 35% of an amount by combining three 10% parts and one 5% part (e.g. 35% of £80 = 24 + 4 = 28).
Explain that this is a general method: name which parts you'd combine to make a different percentage such as 65%.
Use a percentage bar or double number line (100% → 10% → 5% → 35%) to see how the parts make up the whole.
Use a ratio table to scale the 10% and 5% parts to a different total amount, showing the method generalises across amounts, not just one figure.
activities.title: Build a percentage toolkit from 10% and 5%

feedback: If the child only states the shortcut, ask them to explain why ×100 then ÷4 equals ×25, using 25 = 100 ÷ 4.
If the child's explanation holds, ask them to check it against a direct calculation to confirm reasonableness.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent methods and shortcuts are reliable because of structure (25 = 100 ÷ 4), not because they are isolated tricks; understanding why lets you judge when a shortcut applies.
learnerActions: Work out why multiplying any number by 25 can be done by multiplying by 100 then dividing by 4.
Use a factor/equivalent-fraction model (25 = 100 ÷ 4) to explain the equivalence, not just assert it.
Try the method on a worked example and check the result matches the direct multiplication.
Explain in words why the two routes must give the same answer.
activities.title: Justify an equivalent calculation method

feedback: Listen for a position-to-term rule (term = 4×position + 1, so the 20th is 81) reached by linking the constant difference 4 to the position, plus a check against a known term — using the rule to jump rather than counting on is the target.

If the child uses a proportional shortcut (scaling a known term by the position ratio), have them test it on an early known term so the mishandled start-offset is exposed — e.g. 4×(the 5th term) gives 4×21 = 84, whereas the true 20th term is 81. The gap of 3 appears because scaling multiplies the +1 offset by 4 as well (4×1 = 4 instead of 1), so the answer is 3 too big.
There is no single scored answer here; the goal is reasoning that is general and self-checked.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a rule is not enough; its generality must be tested against far cases and known terms, and proportional shortcuts that wrongly scale the constant offset along with the term fail these checks.
learnerActions: Answer 'how would you find the 100th term — does your method still work?' to test whether a rule is genuinely general.
Evaluate a classmate's claim: 'the 20th term is 4×(the 5th term) — is that right? check it on the 2nd term' and explain the flaw.
Explain how to build 35% of £80 from 10% and 5%, and whether the same method gives 65%.
Explain why ×25 equals ×100 then ÷4.
activities.title: Probe and discuss the generality of a rule
